hist: By 1911, the mine had already been abandoned for a number of years. Ore produced from 1911 to 1917 was sent elsewhere for treatment. Glenbar Mines Ltd took out an option over the mine in 1917 and apointed WR Scougall as manager.

WH Crew and party applied for a claim in 1924. The machinery was dismantled in 1925 and a 5-head stamper battery was erected in 1926. Minor production occurred in 1926 and 1927. The Mines Department took over the machinery in 1928.

Scougall and party took over in 1928 and cleaned out Scougall's shaft. Development work was carried out on newly discovered reefs and leaders. The plant was overhauled in 1932 but the water supply gave out. The plant was moved to Running Ck

The Melanie Gold Mining Co formed in 1933 and erected winding gear, 5-head battery and treatment plant. Treatment methods proved unsuccessful. The company was liquidated in 1934. Machinery was sold to the South Burnett syndicate in Kilkivan

per.c: Production figures incomplete; could be more than double that recorded here. Production was generally lumped with other mines worked by the Queensland Copper Company Ltd.

hist: Discovered by Henry Dingle in 1867 or 1869. Minor prospecting and development at Ebenezer workings.

Acquired by Mount Perry Copper Company, with Captain Osborne as mine manager. Reverberatory furnaces commissioned in 1873 and Georges Shaft excavated. The mine was shut down and the company liquidated in 1877.

Purchased by Sir Thomas McIlwraith, with Israel Bennett as mine manager. Mining languished, with brief revivals in 1884 and 1887 to 1889. The railway was completed in 1884. The smelters closed in 1890.

The Queensland Copper Company Ltd purchased the property in 1901. The old furnaces were demolished and new water-jacket furnaces were commissioned in 1902. The Georges and Kennedy shafts were worked, with Alan Gibb as mine manager.

The Milne became the main working shaft in 1909. A small concentrating plant was erected in 1910. Mining and smelting stopped temporarily in 1911 when the company was wound up and reconstituted as the New Queensland Copper Company Ltd.

A 3000 pounds grant from the Mines Department allowed development work to continue. Prices improved in 1912 and production and smelting recommenced in July. The company was forced into liquidation at the end of 1913.
The Milne Shaft was worked by tributers from 1914 to 1917, when the workings were abandoned and flooded. The buildings and machinery were sold in 1919.
The Queensland Copper Company Pty Ltd was treating dump material from the Ebenezer workings to recover copper sulphides.

hist: The Normanby Company was established before the end of 1871, with Captain Hosking as mine manager. Copper was sent to Maryborough. In 1875, the company was restructured as the New Normanby Copper Mining Company.
Worked on tribute by Kelly and son.

The Normanby Syndicate took up an option in 1899 and purchased the Mineral Freehold in 1901. The company worked from the Lazarus Shaft. Eleven parties of tributers worked from separate shafts in 1904.

The Queensland Copper Company Ltd purchased the freehold in 1905 and sank the Pulbrook Shaft to 67m. The shaft was deepened to 112.8m in 1906 and a winze was sunk to prove payable ore to 137.2m depth in 1907.
Lazarus Shaft worked by tributers.

Clarey & party took up the Valda claim in 1932 and erected a 5-head battery. A Gibbs took up the Mundic claim in 1933 to cyanide the Lazarus dumps. Schultz & party worked the Valda in 1934, when the Mundic was abandoned after Gibbs' death.

The Perseverance Prospecting Syndicate (Hunter, Clarey & party) sank the Perseverance Shaft to 22.9m & used the Pulbrook for dewatering & the Lazarus for hauling. Two-head battery erected in 1938 to treat dumps. Results were unsatisfactory.

A.H. Clarey, T.J. Porter and L.D. Barber held the New Dawn claim. The Perseverance Shaft was sunk to 36.9m, with levels at 22.9m and 36.9m in unworked ground. No appreciable ore quantities were found.
exp: The Pulbrook Shaft dump was estimated to contain 7200m3. Samples assayed 1.46-5.43ppm Au, 11-34ppm Ag and 61-210ppm As. The Lazarus dumps were estimated to contain 1700m3. Samples assayed 4.63-6.27ppm Au, 10-11ppm Ag and 36-92ppm As.

hist: Gold was discovered in 1886 and 10 claims were taken up. Gold was only found on the P.C. and Kents Knob. The other claims were abandoned in 1889.

Mount Shamrock Gold Mining Company bought the PC & expended large sums on development. A 20-head stamper was erected, along with a chlorination works & small roasting furnace to recover Bi oxide. The company ceased working the mine in 1894.

The mine was let on tribute. In 1896, it passed into the hands of an Englishman from whom the Mount Shamrock company had borrowed money. The battery recommenced operations in 1897 and the mine was worked on tribute until 1900.
The Mount Shamrock Syndicate erected a cyaniding plant in 1901 and sold off the old machinery. A 10-head battery was erected in 1903. Hard rock ore and tailings were treated up until 1908.

The mine was under exemption until 1911, when prospecting work commenced and the plant was repaired. Gold was produced from hard rock ore and by cyaniding tailings up until 1919, when all mining ceased.

C Martin commenced operations in 1923 and overhauled the machinery and erected a slimes plant. He treated slimes and crushed surface stone from in and around the mill. The shaft was dewatered down to the winze at the 79.2m level.

The mine was dewatered in 1932 to sample the 76.2m level. Mount Shamrock Gold Mines Ltd commenced operations in July 1933. The old crushing plant was removed and a boiler engine, Empire Mill, lighting plant and 5 cyanide vats were erected.
Cyaniding of the old tailings commenced in October 1933. The mine was acquired by Commonwealth Gold Development Ltd in November.
The mine was dewatered to its lowest level and old stopes were mined. The mine closed in November 1934 pending geological investigations. No work was done after an inspection by JH Reid in 1935.
Palmer and Goronszy treated tailings on the Try Again and Same Again claims.

481409.name: BOOLOUMBA CREEK AREA
hist: Narrow alluvial flats and pockets along Booloomba Creek were worked.

About 2.8 kg of gold was won during 1932 to 1934. Five Prospecting Areas on Bollomba Creek were inspected by Government Geologist J.E.Ridgeway in 1934. Small-scale work was practically confined to the creek fronts but reference was made to
adjacent flats up to 20 m wide.

481414.name: DURHAM'S
hist: Prospecting Area 949 was granted to D.R.A. Stephens in June 1926 and transferred to T.C. Thompsen in September 1930. Two tunnels driven in granite. Main shaft known as Marsh's Tunnel.
A small two head stamper battery was erected at the mine. Tunnel at Marsh's leader advanced from 24 m to 48m. Crosscuts put in at 42.6 m and 24m.

Lucky Hit tunnel driven 12.2 m in 1934. Marsh's tunnel stopped in 1935 due to poor air. Lucky Hit driven to 18.2m in 1935. Another tunnel 54.8 m SW of Marsh's started in 1935. Durham Reef prospected in 1938 to 1939.

481418.name: CHINAMAN CREEK

481419.name: COMET MINE

per.c: Production records incomplete. Amount of ore produced is approximate only.

hist: Government Geologist C.C. Morton inspected the workings in 1934 and described a 12.2 m long adit and 9 m deep shaft plus underground workings. A second adit was driven, against the advice of Morton and this drive met the reef only 3 m belo
w the old adit level. It seemed possible to develop the mine further on a limited scale.
The lower adit and two winzes were rehabilitated in 1976 by the lessee, Mr A. Faber and were described by Government geologist N. Krosch in 1977. THe workings collapsed before they could be extended.
Messrs Allen, Marks and Rae drove a new adit at a level 9 to 11 m lower. The southernmost of the old winzes was met 57 m from the portal. and the reef was lost at 81 m.

hist: Discovered by Jack White of Rosebud Station in 1904. James Reid purchased 7 leases (Balaclava, Sebastapal, Greater Esmond, Inkerman, Grand Central, Wallaroo and Wee MacGregor) in 1905. The MacGregor Cloncurry copper MInes Ltd formed.
Stores and dwellings erected. By the end of 1906, a shaft sinking headframe and winding engine were installed. The prospecting shaft was 39.6m deep within 6 months.

Mainly prospecting and development work. The "Wee MacGregor Tramway Agreement Act 1912", proposing a rail link to the mine, was passed by the Queensland Government. The mine passed into the hands of the Hampden Cloncurry Copper Mines Ltd.

The township of Hightville was surveyed. A 35km long 3'6" gauge railway was constructed from Devoncourt to a railhead at Ballara. A 5km 2' gauge tramline to the mine, including a 77m long tunnel, was proposed and construction began in 1914.

The line was commissioned in June 1915, when the Krause locomotive, with 50 tons of ore, made its first trip to the transfer ramp at Ballara. The ore was then railed by Government train to the Kuridala smelters.

The main shaft was deepened to 146.3m in 1981 but intersected a very large water inflow. Mining operations ceased in 1920 after the closure of the Kuridala smelters. The 2' gauge tramway was pulled up and stored at Ballara in 1921.
Intermittent small-scale production by Edna May Mines.

Lease purchased by Eastern Copper Mines NL in 1971. A copper leaching and precipitation plant was set up and the main shaft was reconditioned. 100 x 20m deep solution-injection holes were drilled at 8m intervals along the lode outcrop.
In-situ leaching and copper precipitation in long concrete tanks started in 1974 but was suspended in 1975 due to low copper prices.
Mine reopened by Phillips Metals Exploration Company Pty Ltd (as managers for eastern Copper Mines) and operated until 1979. Production was about 18t of 90% Cu cement per month.
Minor copper production.

hist: The Normanby Company was established by the end of 1871, with Captain Hosking as mine manager. The company worked the Palmer, Moore and Graham shafts and Frazers Tunnel. Copper was sent to Maryborough.
The Normanby Company was restructured as the New Normanby Copper Mining Company in 1875.

The Queensland Copper Company Ltd acquired the Mineral Freehold in 1904 and began work on the Palmer Shaft. By 1907, the Palmer shaft was the largest single copper producer on the field. The mine closed down in July 1911 due to poor prices.

In 1912, the Native Copper Shaft was deepened to 151.5m and the smelters resumed operations. Drives connected the Native Copper and Palmer shafts. Tributers worked the mine from 1915 to 1919, when the machinery and buildings were sold.
Dunn and son excavated a 60.6m long adit, with a 14.2m deep shaft near the portal, at their New Hit mine above the Palmer Shaft.

hist: ROFFEY & PARTY APPLIED FOR PAs IN 1932. COMMENCED DEWATERING THE MINE IN 1933. SAMPLING IN 1934. THE PROPERTY WAS UNDER OPTION TO AN ENGLISH COMPANY FROM 1936 TO 1938 AND TO J J GANLY IN 1938. HUNTER & PARTY REOPENED OLD WORKINGS IN 1939.
GAETA GOLD MINING LEASE SYNDICATE WORKED THE MINE IN 1940. A BATTERY AND PUMPING PLANT WERE ERECTED. A SOUTH BURNETT SYNDICATE WORKED THE MINE IN 1942.

THE MILLER SYNDICATE OPENED UP A SECTION OF THE MINE IN 1946 & ERECTED A WINDING PLANT AND POPPET HEAD AT MILLERS NO.1 SHAFT. TAILINGS WERE TREATED IN 1947. THERE IS NO RECORD OF ANY WORKING OF THE MINE AFTER 1947.

GAETA PIONEER GOLD MINING COMPANY FORMED IN 1904. MAIN SHAFT SUNK TO 57.9M AND A STEAM WINDING PLANT ERECTED. J D ANDERSON ERECTED A 5 HEAD BATTERY. SIGNIFICANT UNDERGROUND DEVELOPMENT FOLLOWED. CYANIDING PLANT SET UP IN 1905.
THE GAETA PIONEER GOLD MINING COMPANY WENT INTO LIQUIDATION IN 1907.
THE WORKINGS WERE DEWATERED IN 1909. ONLY MINOR WORK WAS CARRIED OUT. THE MINE WAS WORKED ON TRIBUTE TO THE GAETA PIONEER MINING COMPANY LTD IN 1912.
THE PIONEER REEF WAS DISCOVERED BY HAINE, GOSSNER AND LAHEY IN APRIL 1880. THE PHOENIX AND LADY MABEL MILLS, EACH WITH 10 HEAD OF STAMPS, WERE OPERATNG BY 1881. A LACK OF WATER HAMPERED PRODUCTION.

THE FIELD WAS ESSENTIALLY ABANDONED IN 1883. THE MINERS WERE UNABLE TO SUCCESSFULLY TREAT THE SULPHIDE ORE. THE PHOENIX BATTERY WAS REMOVED FROM THE FIELD. VERY LITTLE WORK DONE. THE GAETA GOLD & MINERAL FIELD WAS PROCLAIMED IN 1898.

hist: Gold was discovered by a bullock driver in 1892. A syndicate then took up the ground as the Yorkeys Surprise. Shafts and extensive underground workings were excavated. Ore was treated at Gympie until a 10-head battery was erected in 1899.
The Yorkeys Surprise Marodian Syndicate purchased the mine in 1901. The block shaft was sunk in 1902.
The mine was let on tribute to White and party, who cyanided the tailings. Peteron brothers carried out cyaniding of tailings under tribute in 1906.
